(a) to (e) Yes, Sir. Andhra Pradesh State Housing Corporation (APSHC) had 
tentatively indicated that a total of 53473 dwelling

units would be taken up in 20 towns of Andhra Pradesh under the VAMBAY 
scheme. However, they have submitted a proposal for construction of 4000

inability of other States/UTs to make full use of their allocations in the current 
financial year, is also likely. More funds will be available to the State in the 
coming financial years.

grateful to the Hon. Prime Minister for launching the Valmiki Ambedkar

houses during 2001-2002, but only 4,000 houses were sanctioned. It is a

Pradesh and sanction 50,000 houses during 2001-2002, as requested by our 
Chief Minister. Part (b) of my question is whether the hon.  Minister will 
clarify — there is a discrepancy  in the figures

Independence, it is for the first time that this kind of a scheme has been

Rs. 100 crores, the Ministry of Finance have released only Rs. 69 crores. The

the population of the slums in the town.

like  to  tell  him,  whatever  is  the

SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Sir, due to floods, every 
year a large number of houses of poor people are destroyed in villages and 
towns alongside seacqast and rivers. Sir, I think they also deserve assistance under 
the Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) along with urban slums. My 
question is : Will the hon. Minister kindly assure the House that cases of flood 
victims also will be considered for giving assistance under the VAMBAY? 
SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA: Sir, the Valmiki Ambedkar Awas 
Yojana (VAMBAY) is mainly meant for the urban poor people. But, even 
semi-urban areas, where there are big slums, are also included in it. However, 
the thing is that the main priority will be given to the flood-affected people, as 
has been requested by the poor people, particularly the flood-affected people 
of Andhra Pradesh. Recently, Rayalase ema, Cuddapah, Nellore districts and 
other area have been affected by floods. These districts have also been 
covered under it. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether it is a fact that the Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, an integral 
sanitation programme, is a part of the VAMBAY, and covering only State 
capitals and major cities and not extending to the other urban cities and district 
headquarters. If so, I would like to know the reasons for such restrictions because, 
the VAMBAY is being taken up in all the districts. If you do not extend this 
Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan to other districts and towns, how ate you going to provide 
sanitary facilities in those districts where projects under the VAMBAY have 
been taken up? The hon. Minister may kindly explain. 
SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA: Sir, under the Valmiki Ambedkar 
Awas Yojana, one component is, sanitation programme, because a lot of sanitation 
facilities are required in the slum areas of our country. The poor people are living 
under inhuman conditions in slum areas, which result in many health hazards. 
That is why, we 
4 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
have included this Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan as one component of the Valmiki 
Ambedkar Awas Yojana. Sir, this Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan is a sanitation 
programme for the slums in the country. Out of the funds allocated under the 
VAMBAY, 20 per cent will go to the sanitation programme. This year, i.e., 
2002-03, the Budget allocation for the VAMBAY programme is Rs. 256.85 
crores. Out of this amount, 20 per cent of the amount will go to the National 
Sanitation Programme, i.e., Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan. Firstly, under this 
Programme, we wanted to take up major metropolitan cities. There are six 
metropolitan cities which have got the highest slum population. The second 
category is the million-plus cities which constitute 37 per cent of the slum 
population. These million-plus cities ar e located mostly in capital cities and 
bigger cities. For example, in Andhra Pradesh, Kurnool, Visakhapatnam, 
Vijayawada, etc. As far as this problem is concerned, money is not a constraint. 
That is why we wanted to concentrate mainly on those areas where there is a 
maximum slum population. We should concentrate on those areas. That is why, it 
is done in a phased manner. Also, with the Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, we have 
another programme for sanitation, a slum improvement programme. We call it 
the National Slum Development Programme. NSDP. Under the NSDP also, the 
Urban Development Ministry, every y ear, is allocating Rs. 350 crores. 
Together with the Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan and the VAMBAY programme, this 
NSDP is also there and we are going to take up the sanitation programme. 
DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Sir, many schemes, which are meant for 
the poor, are being misused by many governmental organisations. Now, my 
specific question to the Minister is this. Is there any special machinery to 
identify the bona fide beneficiaries of this scheme? 
SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA: Sir, this Valmiki Ambedkar Awas 
Yojana will be monitored by State Governments. Title is the biggest problem for 
the slum dwellers. Land is a State subject. That is why the scheme is executed by 
the District Urban Development Authorities or the Slate Development Authorities 
in the States. Also, we have invited many of the reputed NGOs. Through NGOs 
also, we 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
want to take up this scheme. But, the hon. Member has rightly pointed out 
that there is misuse of the funds. Particularly, when SO per cent subsidy is 
coming to the poorer sections, in the name of poor people, a lot of 
exploitation is taking place. Taking this into consideration, we want to take 
up the scheme through NGOs. Secondly, th is scheme has got reservation. We 
will not allow even the State Governments to divert the funds. That is why we 
have put two conditions. One condition is, reservation. Under this 
reservation, SO per cent will be for the SC and ST people; 30 per cent will be 
for the OBCs; 15 per cent will be for other weaker sections; and five per cent 
will be for handicapped persons. Like that, we have reservations. The next 
condition is very, very important. It relates to title. The State Government has 
to give the title. Therefore, the two conditions relate to reservation and the 
title of the land. These two things are taken care of in this way. Definitely, I 
assure the hon. Member, we will take care of the misuse of the scheme.

SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, there are tw o limbs of the supplementary. The 
first limb is that out of the 93 occas ions on which the Constitution has been 
amended, the hon. Member is very right that a large number of those 
amendments have actually been of a nature where dates or some period had to 
be extended; but there have been certain substantial amendments as well.

when they give their final recommendations on these, I am sure, this whole question 
of hidden Agenda or unhidden agenda would be clarified. After 50 years of the 
Indian Constitution, it is time to pause and lookback and see how we can 
strengthen some of our institutions created through our Constitution itself. And,

support of two-thirds of the Members present in the House. So, unless he supports it,

identify persons suffering from various mental disorders and epilepsy and

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) According to analysis done by the National Drug 
Dependence Treatment Centre, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New 
Delhi, of the National Sample Survey Data (52nd Round conducted in 1995) 
the prevalence of alcohol consumption in  rural and urban areas of Karnataka 
is slightly above the national average. In rural areas, the lowest prevalence of 
alcohol consumption is 0.4% in Lakshadweep and 1.7% in Haryana and the 
highest is 46.2% in Arunachal Pradesh. In urban areas the lowest

and Family Welfare was set up. This Task Force has submitted its final report

Illegal sex determination 
*209. SHRI SATISH PR ADHAN: Will the Minist er of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that large scale illegal sex determination in the 
country is leading female foeticide resulting in a serious imbalance in the 
male-female sex ratio brought out by the Census 2001; 
(b) if so, the response of Government  thereto and the corrective steps 
taken/proposed to be taken in this regard; and 
(c) the action taken or proposed to be taken against clinics which are 
using ultrasound machines without licence? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) The Census 2001 has revealed that sex ratio in the age 
group of 0-6 years has declined from 945 in 1991 to 927 in 2001. Several 
reasons are adduced for the same. Some of the reasons are: 
• Son preference 
• Neglect of the girl child resulting in their higher mortality at younger age 
• Higher maternal mortality 
• Female infanticide 
• Female foeticide 
• Male bias in enumeration of population. 
With a view to containing the men ace of female foeticide, Government 
has brought into force the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and 
Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994 (PNDT Act) with effect from 1.1.1996. The 
implementation of the provisions of the Act rests with the States/UTs. As the 
implementation of the Act was not satisfactory in various States /UTs, in a 
Public interest Litigation filed by the Centre for Enquiry into Health and 
Allied Themes (CEHAT) & others, the Supreme Court of India has issued 
directions to both Central and State Governments for more effective 
implementation of the Act. The directions of the Supreme Court, inter-alia, 
include generation of awareness about the provisions of the 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
Act both at national, State and district levels, implementation of the Act with 
full vigour and zeal to ensure regist ration of all clinics using ultrasound 
machines so as to keep an eye on th em lest they should undertake sex 
determination of foetus of pregnant woman, obtaining of information relating 
to users of such machines from thei r manufacturers, importers, suppliers, 
dealers, persons having their maintenance contracts and others, scaling and 
seizure of the machines of those who have not got themselves registered 
under the Act, to restrict sale of such machines to registered clinics, to amend 
the Act keeping in mind the emerging technologies and difficulties 
encountered in implementation of the Act and take all other such measures as 
may be necessary for effective implementation of the Act. 
The Central Government have requested all the State Govcrnmcnts/UTs to 
implement the provisions of the Act and comply with the directions of the 
Hon'blc Supreme Court of India with  full vigour and zeal. Appropriate 
Authorities and Advisory Committees have been appointed under the Act in 
all the States/ UTs. These have been a ppointed at district and at some places 
at sub-district levels in most of th e Statcs/UTs. They arc taking action to 
generate awareness about the provisions of the Act in public and among law 
enforcing agencies, service providers, medical and paramedical personnel by 
hoardings, wall paintings, news papers, All India Radio, TV and other means 
of publicity. The Central Government has constituted a Central Supervisory 
Board under the chairmanship of Minist er of Health and Family Welfare. 
Quarterly returns about the implementation of the Act and compliance with 
the directions of the Supreme Court of India are obtained from State 
Govcrnmcnts/UTs and reviewed by the Central Supervisory Board (CSB). 
A list of over 11,000 buyers of ultrasound machines received from the 
manufacturers, importers, suppliers, dealer s, service providers etc. of such 
machines has been forwar ded to the States/UTs for ensuring registration of 
the persons/bodies mentioned in the list including scaling and seizure of the 
machines of unregistered clinics. Th ey have so far filed 103 complaints 
against the violators of the provisions of the Act and have scaled/seized 
machines of 22 clinics.

all the States/ UTs. These have been ap pointed at district and at some places 
at sub-district levels in most of the Statcs/UTs. They arc taking action to 
generate awareness about the provisions of the Act in public and among law 
enforcing agencies, service providers, medical and paramedical personnel by

means  of  publicity.   The   Central

Functioning of Medical System 
1505. SHRI K. KALAVE NKATA RAO: Will the Mi nister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Santosh Medical College , Ghaziabad and D.Y. Medical 
College for Women, Pimpri, Pune are not having full bed occupancy and 
flouting admission quota for NRIs; 
(b) if so, when were the colleges inspected during the last two years by the 
Medical Council of India and what were its observations; and 
(c) the action taken to ensure that functioning of the entire medical system 
in the country is properly regulated? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) During the inspections conducted 
by the Medical Council of India the Sa ntosh Medical College, Ghaziabad and 
D.Y. Patil Medical College for Women, Pimpri, Pune were found to have 
adequate bed occupancy for 50 and 100 admissions annually, respectively. It 
was found that between the academic se ssions of 1995-96 and 1999-2000, 
Santosh Medical College, Ghaziabad had made excess admissions of 40 
students under the Management/NRI quota. The Central Government, taking 
into account the interest of the students, conveyed its approval as a one time 
measure to a proposal received from the college authorities for neutralizing 
the said excess admissions in the succeeding academic sessions by surrendering 
the Management/NRI quota of seats. As per the information available with 
the Government, the D.Y. Patil Medical College for Women, Pimpri, Pune 
has not admitted any students in excess of its capacity. 
(b) The inspections of Santosh Medi cal College, Ghaziabad were carried 
out by the Council Inspectors during the last two years on 12^-14th October, 
2000, 19th & 20th January, 2001 and 16th April, 2001. The inspections of 
Dr. D.Y. Patil Medical College for Women, Pimpri, Pune were carried out by 
the Council Inspectors during the last two years on 9th & 10th June, 2000, 
26th—28th December, 2000 and 2nd-3rd April, 2001. After being satisfied 
that these Colleges 
88 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
fulfilled the prescribed minimum requirements in terms of infrastructure and 
other facilities, the Medical Council of India recommended to the Central 
Government for recognition of the MBBS degree awarded to the students being 
trained in both these colleges by the concerned affiliating Universities. 
(c) The Medical Council of India, with the approval of the Central Government, 
prescribes the minimum standards of medical education required for grant of both 
graduate and postgraduate medical qualifications by the Universities and 
medical institutions in the country. The Council conducts periodic inspections of 
the medical institutions for this purpose. It also takes necessary follow up action 
to ensure that the deficiencies pointed oujt in the inspection reports are rectified 
by the concerned medical institution.

Availability of health services to rural women and children 
1509. SHRIMATI BASANTI SARMA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that health se rvices available to rural women and 
children arc at par with those of urban areas; 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor; and

health services in rural areas in the country? 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA) (a) and (b) Government always 
endeavours to provision for quality of care in delivering basic and essential health 
services to women and children in both urban and rural areas. However, on account 
of constraints of difficult terrain, remote locations, distances, difficult 
communication systems and poor transportation facilities in rural areas, the utilization 
of these services by the people, remains in-adequate. 
(c) Government is taking steps to help State Governments to improve 
integrated service delivery in the rural areas. 
(i) Under the State Health Systems Project, the Community Health Centres 
and District Hospitals are being upgraded and better equipped to provide 
quality health services to people in rural and backward areas. 
(ii) Under the Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana, specific provisioning has 
been made towards repairs and renovation of the public health 
infrastructure, purchasing of drugs and essential consumables, and 
contingencies.

assistance from external agencies for strengthening of health and family 
welfare infrastructure. One of the main activities of Area Projects 
includes construction of buildings for sub-centres, primary health centres 
and community health centres.

Information,  Education and Communication activities undertaken by 
National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) 
Electronic Media 
NACO is utilizing the massive outreach of Doordarshan and private 
satellite channel for telecast of messages on HIV/AIDS prevention and 
control during prime time. These include messages on sexually transmitted 
diseases, blood safety and "voluntary blood donation. Some of the specific 
activities arc as follows: 
Spirit of Unity Concert 
NACO has sponsored a classical mu sic programme "Spirit of Unity 
Concerts" to mainstream the issue of  HIV/AIDS and to reach out to the 
cultural elite and other educated classes through this programme. 
Telecast of Madhuri Dixit spots 
Spots made by the renowned film maker Shri Jabbar Patcl featuring the 
popular film star Madhur i Dixit have been telecast on prime time channels. 
The objectives is to cr eate awareness and empower women to discuss the 
difficult issue of HIV/AIDS in the family and prevent further spread of the 
infection. 
Campaign for Youth 
NACO developed two audio and two video spots focusing on the 
vulnerability of young people to HIV. Press advertisements were also 
developed as part of this campaign. 
Talk Show 
Interactive communication, publicity of best practices and sharing of 
experiences is an important communication strategy for the prevention and 
control of HIV/AIDS. NACO has produced a talk show hosted by celebrities 
such as Mallika Sarabhai and Nccna Gupta for the urban and rural audiences. 
This has been telecast on Doordarshan and Zee News. 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
Att India Radio 
A special programme, in the drama mode, has been devised for rural and 
migrant youth. The programme which is titled "jiyo Aur Jeene Do" is being 
broadcast on 45 commercial broadcasting stations of AIR since June, 1998, The 
ten minutes programme is broadcast in 20 languages on Tuesday evening at 
8.00 P.M. 
AIR-FM 
NACO is using the popular FM channel to combine entertainment and 
education in reaching out to the urban youth. The one hour programme which is 
tilled "NACO Film Hit Parade" is broadcast for one hour every week on the AIR-
FM channel in Delhi. 
Rural Outreach and Press Activities 
Since, 1994, the Song and Drama Division of Government of India has been 
involved in the AIDS awareness campaign. It has produced several street plays, 
songs and dramas and has performed in 400 different locations utilizing the 
local drama troupes in many States. The Directorate of Field Publicity bas also 
participated in the campaign. AH its 260 field units located have conducted 
several programmes such as seminars, debate/essay and quiz competitions and 
film shows for AIDS awareness. 
The Press Information Bureau of tbc Government of India has organized a 
number of programmes to sensitize the regional press on the issue of HIV/AIDS. 
National AIDS Telephone Helpline 
A toll free National AIDS Telephone Helpline has been set up to provide 
access to information and counselling on  HIV/AIDS related issues, this is a 
computerized four digit number, 1097, with a voice response system linked with 
the telephonic hotline. This is a very popular service at 77 locations in the 
country. 
School AIDS Education Programme 
Young people are among the most vulnerable to HIV/AIDS. Sc hool AIDS 
Education is one of the important programmes that focuses towards student 
youth to raise awareness levels, help young

prograaune reinforces family values and respect for the opposite sex. The

referral   services,   if

1524. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: W ill the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the standard of health facilities available in the 
country are a third that of Thailand's which just meet the WHO minimum standard 
of health care for developing countries; 
(b) whether India have just one doctor per 3000 people and the ratio has to 
be brought down to one for just at least 500 people; 
(c) whether a two-day health summit was held on 25th and 26th February, 2002 
in New Delhi in order to evolve a comprehensive plan on the health care sector; 
and 
(d) if so, what are its recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) According to the World Health 
Report, 2000 although India has been ranked below Thailand in terms of overall 
health systems performance, it would be erroneous to conclude that standard of 
health facilities available in the country are third of that existing in Thailand, as 
the various parameters used in the Report are amorphous and subjective. Also, 
the methodology used in assessing these parameters for the purpose of ranking 
countries is unscientific, non representative and inaccurate. In view of the above, 
the reliability of the findings is questionable. 
(b) The doctor-population ratio at present works out to approximately 
1:1800 in respect of allophathic doctors. However, including around 6 lakh 
qualified medical practitioners in other systems of medicines like Ayurveda, 
Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy, the ratio comes down to 1:800. This ratio is 
sufficient to take care of health care services all over the country. 
(c) and (d) Pursuant to the two day health summit held C II in February, 2002. 
Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) has taken up a study with the overall 
objective of defining a roadmap for the health care sector in India, leading to 
its accelerated development.

Maternal Mortality Rate 
This is defined as the number of maternal deaths on account of pregnancy, 
childbirth or within 42 days of childbirth per 1,00,000 live births. 
Estimates of maternal mortality rate are available for the National level 
and some major States from the Sample Registration System of the Registrar

Perinatal Mortality Rate 
This is defined as the number of still births (born dead) plus infant deaths 
of less than seven days for every 1000 live births during the year. 
The estimates for Perinatal Mortality Rate for India and major States are 
available from the SRS of Registrar General of India for the years 1996 to 
1998. These are given at Statement-II (See below). 
Maternal Health and Child Health are an integral part of the Reproductive 
and Child Health Programme and aims at bringing down the maternal, infant 
and child mortality and morbidity. Under

8. Facilities and training for medical termination of pregnancies for- safe

Programme for Maternal and Child Health through the mass media as also

All-India network to tackle fatal diseases 
1533. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal with Government to have All-India 
network to tackle fatal diseases; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) As a Public Health 
measure, Government of India has been implementing various National 
Health Programmes. The National Surveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases is one of these programmes. The National 
Surveillance Programme for Communicable Diseases was launched as a pilot 
programme in 1997-1998 in 5 districts (one each in Kerala, Karnataka, 
Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat) with  a view to strengthen the disease 
surveillance system so that early warning signals of outbreak arc recognized 
and appropriate follow-up action is initiated. The programme is being 
implemented through the existing health infrastructure programme and 
surveillance system involving training of medical and para-medical personnel, 
upgradation of laboratories, and improvement in communication system. The 
programme is currently implemented in 80 districts. 
Under the Tenth Five Year Plan, a pr oject Implementation Plan, integrating 
various activities under the programme is envisaged to be prepared so as to 
strengthen the existing surveillance syst em at the district, State and National 
levels and to build up additional capacities for effective communication and 
technology, upgradation of laboratories etc., ensure involvement of public and 
private sector institutions, private practitioners and NGOs in the process of 
effective implementation  of disease  surveillance  programme.  This 
136 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
would integrate non-communicable diseases also in the programme, 
develop proper urban surveillance systems, and utilization of 
available resources and to bring abou t effective inter-sect oral cooperation 
among various agencies in the Health and Non-Health Sector.

† 1535. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the report which 
appeared in the Jansatta, dated 22nd February, 2002 in which it has been 
stated that the number of heart-patients is higher amongst the pre-natals in 
the case of women who arc living in metropolitan cities/urban areas; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the grou ps of doctors of University of 
California, Los Angles School of Public Health and California Birth Defects 
Monitoring Programme has stated that it will lead to grave consequences, if

effect of air pollution on the occurrence of birth defects and have found that 
pregnant women exposed to air pollution are at higher risk of having babies

smoking, occupational exposures, vitamin supplement use, diet and obesity.

Medical care in rural areas 
1536. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have, so far, chalked out any time-bound 
programme to provide medical care in remote rural areas in States like 
Rajasthan and Orissa, in particular and other States in general; 
(b) whether Government are aware th at health care industry has a 
potential of creating 30 million jobs in the country; and 
(c) if so, what steps Government have taken so far to harness the 
potential of health care industry in generating employment besides health 
checking programmes, particularly in above-mentioned States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Yes, Sir. Health Care Service in 
rural and remote areas of the country  including Rajasthan and Orissa are 
provided through a system of Primary Health Care Infrast ructure including 
Sub-centres, Primary Health Centres and Community Health Centres. The 
Central Government supplements the efforts of the State Government to 
strengthen Health Care Services with the following interventions. 
(i) Under the State Health System s Project, the Community Health 
Centres and District Hospitals arc being upgraded and better 
equipped to provide quality health services to people in rural and 
backward areas. 
(ii) Under the Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana, specific funds are 
allocated towards the repair and renovation of the public health 
infrastructure, purchasing of drugs and essential consumables as 
well as towards contingencies. 
(iii) Area Development Project are being implemented with financial 
assistance from external agencies fo r addressing gaps in integrated 
service delivery through the construction of buildings for sub-
centres, primary health centres and community health centres. 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
(iv) Under the Reproductive and Child Health Programme, the following 
steps are being taken to strengthen the primary health services in the 
Country: 
 Major Civil Works for repair/construction of OT/Labour Room 
  Provision of equipments/medicine for emergency obstetric care at 
first referral units 
 Financial assistance for contract appointment/hiring of 
Anesthetists/Gynaecologists/Safe Motherhood consultants/ Staff 
Nurses/Lab. Technician, Additional ANMs etc. 
 Skill based in-service training for capacity building of ANMs and 
other health functionaries. 
Efforts are also being made to increase the outreach of health care services 
through Swasthya Melas and Reproductive and Child Health camps etc. 
Rajasthan and Orissa have been incl uded in the list of Empowered Action 
Group States focus attention on addressing the unmet need for basic and 
essential health care services through the implementation of area specific 
programmes and partnership with voluntary associations, community 
organizations and panchayatiraj institutions. 
It is further envisaged that village self-help groups be utilized to organize 
and provide basic services for Reproductive and Child Health care, combined 
with the ongoing Integrated child of Development Scheme. Aanganwadi 
Centres could become the center for disseminating basic health care activities, 
contraceptive counseling as well as supply, nutrition, education and 
supplementation as well as pre-school activities. These could also function as 
depots for ORS/ basic medicines and contraceptives. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. Government are aware that health care industry has a 
potential of creating a large number of jobs in the country. The Government 
alone cannot meet all the health needs of the people. With this in view, 
collaboration with the industry is proposed. The following operational strategies 
have been envisaged which would al so generate employment besides 
improving health care: 
1. The corporate sector and industry could, for instance, take on 
140 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SAB HA 
the challenge of strengthening the management information systems in the 
seven most deficient States , at district hospitals and primary health center 
levels by introducing electronic data entry machines to lighten the tedious 
work load of ANMs and the multi-purpose workers at sub-centres and the 
doctors at the primary health centers, while targeting wider coverage and 
outreach. 
2. Collaborate with non-Government s ectors in running professionally 
sound advertisement and marketing campaigns for products an services, 
targeting all segments of the population, from village level upwards, in other 
words, strengthen advocacy and IEC, including social marketing of 
contraceptives. 
3. Provide markets to sustain the income-generating activities from 
village levels upwards. In turn, this will ensure corisistent motivation among 
the community for pursuing health and education-related community 
activities. 
4. Help promote transportation to re mote and inaccessible areas from 
village levels upwards. 
5. The social responsibilities of the corporate sector in industry must, at 
the very minimum, extend to providing preventing reproductive and child 
health care for its own employees (if 100 workers are engaged). 
6. Create a national network consisting of voluntary, public, private and 
non-Government health centres, identified by a common logo, for delivering 
reproductive and child health services, free to any client. The provider will 
be compensated for the service provided, on the basis of a coupon system, 
duly counter-signed by the beneficiary and paid for by a system that will be 
fully articulated. The compensation will be identical to providers, across all 
sectors. The end user exercises choices  in the source of service delivery. A 
committee of management experts will be set up to devise ways of ensuring 
that this system is not abused. 
7. From a consortium of the voluntary sector, the non-Government sector 
and the private corporate sector to aid Government in the 
141

education. 
8. In the area of basic education, set up privately run/managed primary

up/managed by the panchayat, the private corporate sector could provide the 
mid-day meals, the text-books and/or the uniforms.

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) The operation of the cable 
television networks in the country are governed by the provisions of the 
Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and Rules framed 
thereunder. The Act, inter-alia, provides for manadatory registration of cable 
operators and does not envisage any restrictions on the number of operators in

Cleansing of the legal profession 
1570. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: 
SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): 
Will the Minister of LAW, JU STICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the recent 
Supreme Court verdict concerning the need to cleanse the legal profession;      
(b) if so, the background and details thereof; 
(c) whether any specific modifications arc proposed to be made in the 
related Advocates Law; and 
(d) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) and (b) In Harish Chandra Tiwari Vs. Baiju 
[(2002) 2 Supreme Court Cases 67], the Supreme 
174 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Court imposed the punishment of removal of the name of the appellant from 
the roll of advocates for a -grave professional miscounduct on his part in that 
he had misappropriated the amount of compensation awarded to his client. 
The Supreme Court held that the punishment of suspending the advocate 
from practice for a period of three years, imposed by the Disciplinary 
Committee of the Bar Council of India, was not sufficient. Where the 
delinquent advocate returns the money misappropriated before commencing 
the disciplinary proceedings, a lesser pu nishment may be justified. In the 
instant case, the misappropriation remain ed unabated. In th is context, the 
Supreme Court observed that there was a need to cleanse the legal 
profession. 
(c) and (d) Section 35 of the Advocates Act, 1961 already prescribes three 
kinds of punishments for professional or other misconduct on the part of an 
advocate, namely: (i) reprimand the advocate; (ii) suspend the advocate from 
practice for such period as may be deemed fit; and (iii) remove the name of 
the advocate from the State roll of advocates. The observations of the 
Supreme Court in the above case have been noted. The Government feel that 
there is no need to change the Advocates Act, 1961.

Status of Employees of three organs of Government 
1573. SHRI BANARASI DAS GUPTA: Will the Minister of LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have three main organs i:e., 
Executive, Parliament and Judiciary; 
(b) if so, whether the employees of these organs are Central Government 
employees; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) Executive, Parliament (Legislature) and 
Judiciary are three wings of the Stat e and not of the Government (the 
Executive) vide State of Bihar v. Bihar Distilleries Ltd., [(1997) 2 SCC 453]. 
(b) and (c) While dealing with the question whether members of the 
Gujarat Panchayat Service under Gujarat Panchayat Act, 1961 were 
Government servant or not, the Constitution bench of the Supreme Court in 
State of Gujarat v. Raman Lil Keshav Lal Soni [(1983) 2 SCC 33] has laid 
down the following criteria to determ ine whether an employee is employee 
of the Government or not:— 
"We do not propose and indeed it is neither politic nor possible to lay 
down any definite test to determine when a person may be said to hold a 
civil post under the Government. Several factors may indicate the 
relationship of master and servant. None may be conclusive. On the other 
hand, no single factor may be consider ed absolutely essential. The presence 
of all or some of the factors such as, the right to select for appointment, the 
right to appoint, the right to terminate the employment, the right to take other 
disciplinary action, the right to prescribe the conditions of service, the nature 
of the duties performed by the employee, the right to control the employee's 
manner and method of the work, the right to issue directions and the 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
right to determine and the source from which wages or salary are 
paid and a host of such circumstances, may have to be considered  to 
determine the existences of the relationship of master and 
servant. In each case, it is question of fact whether a person is a 
servant of the State or not."

Corruption in Judiciary 
1578. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned, "Chief Justice admits to graft in Judiciary", which appeared in the 
Hindustan Times, dated the 17th February, 2002; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to address the problem of prevailing 
corruption in the Judiciary highlighted in the report? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Hon'ble Chief Justice of  India on 23rd December, 2001 at 
a joint conference organized by the ba r Council of India and the State bar 
Council of Kerala inter-alia stated: 
"...I have said it before and I will say it again: in my opinion, more 
than 80% of the Judges in this co untry, across the board, are honest 
and incorruptible. It is that smaller percentage that brings the entire 
judiciary into disrepute. To make it known that the judiciary does 
not tolerate corruption in its ranks, it is requisite that corrupt Judges 
should be investigated and dismi ssed from service. This is very 
much possible in the case of subordinate judiciary because 
disciplinary control lies with the High Court. It is difficult where the 
higher judiciary is concerned becau se the only recourse in law is 
impeachment, whcih is a cumbersome process and which, as a 
recent instance showed, may not achieve the desired result for 
reasons that are political. The Supreme Court and the High Court 
have attempted to evolve an informal procedure to meet the 
situation, but it is yet to be tested." 
Under article 235 of the Constitution of India, the administrative control 
over the members of subordinate Judici al Service vests with the concerned 
High Court, in exercise of powers conferred under proviso to article 309 read 
with articles 233 and 234 of the Constitution, the State Government frames 
rules and regulations in Consultation with the High Court exercising 
jurisdiction in relation to 
182 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
such State. The members of the State Judicial Service are governed by these 
rules and regulations. 
With regard to corruption in higher judiciary, articles 124(4) and 217(1) of 
the Constitution of India provide that a Judge of the Supreme Court/High 
Court may be removed on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity 
in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Constitution.

1600. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the  Minister of 
SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the seventh disability as listed in the Disability Act of 1995, is 
mental illness and neither his Ministry nor the Commissioner of Persons with 
Disabilities has any clue about its role in the care and management of 
mentally-ill patients; 
(b) if so, whether under this Act there are various ways in which a mentally 
handicapped persons can be gainfully employed but little efforts have been 
made in this direction; 
(c) whether Central Coordination Committee, which is supposed to review 
and coordinate all activities has not met since November, 1998; and 
(d) if so, the main reasons for the same? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JU STICE AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. 
SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): (a) and (b) "Mental Illness" has been 
recognized as a disability under the Persons with Disabilities (Equal 
Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995. The 
Mental Health Act, 1987 containing provisions for care and treatment of 
mentally ill persons is administered by the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare while the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment supports 
voluntary organizations in undertaking rehabilitation programmes for the cured 
mentally ill. Voluntary organizations also run programmes for imparting 
vocational training to the mentally handicapped and run shelter workshops 
for them. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

Finalization of VAMBAY 
1608. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI:  
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have finalized details of the National Scheme 
for slums titled "Valmiki-Ambedkar Awas Yojana"; and 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme and its planning for solving the various 
problems besetting slums? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 'Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY)' was launched with the objective of providing shelter or 
upgrading the existing shelter for the slum-dwellers below the poverty line 
including those belonging to Economically Weaker Sections in urban areas 
with a component of basic sanitation facilities and community toilets. The 
details of the scheme containing the manner of implementation and planning 
for solving the problems of slum dwellers arc given in the statement. 
Statement 
    Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Joyana (Vainbay) 
Shelter is a basic human requirement.  For a shelterless person, getting a 
house brings about a profound social change in status and integrating him with 
his social milieu. The provisional estimates made from 2001 Census indicate 
that while India is urbanising markedly, slums in urban India are increasing 
alarmingly. The slum population in urban India is estimated to be about 62 
million. 
There is at present no housing scheme in the Central Sector for the urban 
poor. There are two Central Sector pr ogrammes targeted towards the urban 
poor, namely the SJSRY and NSDP. The SJSRY attempts to provide 
employment in order to bring the urban poor above the poverty line while 
NSDP is basically a programme for the environmental  improvement  of  
urban  slums.  The  urban  poverty 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
alleviation strategy is incomplete  without  a significant component 
pertaining to housing delivery for the slum dwellers. 
In order to fill this gap in a major policy initiative, the Prime Minister of 
India announced a new Centrally Sponsored Scheme called the Valmiki 
Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) on the 15th August, 2001 to 
ameliorate the conditions of the urban slum dwellers living below poverty 
line. 
The objective of VAMBAY is primarily to provide shelter or upgrade the 
existing shelter for people living below the poverty line in urban slums in a 
march towards the goal of slumlcss cities with a healthy and enabling urban 
environment. The target group under the VAMBAY will be all slum dwellers 
in urban areas who arc below the pov erty line including members of EWS 
who do not possess adequate shelter. 
Another very important basic amenity for slum dwellers especially in 
congested metropolitan cities is the lack  of rudimentary toilet facilities. A 
new National City Sanitation Project under the title of "Nirmal Bharat 
Abhiyan" is an integral sub component of VAMBAY. 20% of the total 
allocation under VAMBAY will be used for the same at the rate of Rs. 200 
crorcs as loan from HUDCO and Rs. 200 crore as subsidy. The State 
Governments/Local Bodies of course will be free to supplement this amount 
with their own grant or subsidy as th e case may be. The average cost for a 
community toilet seat has been estimated to be Rs. 40,000/- per scat. 
Therefore, a 10-seat or a 20-seat to ilet block meant for men, women and 
children with separate compartments  for each group a nd special design 
features will cost around Rs. 4 lakhs or  Rs. 8 lakhs respectively. Each toilet 
block will be maintained by a group fr om among the slum dwellers who will 
make a monthly contribution of about Rs. 20 or so per family and obtain a 
monthly pass or family card. 
During the current financial year; 2001-02, a modest beginning may be 
made with a limited sum of Rs. 100 crore made available out of the savings 
of the Ministry of Urban Development. However, during the 10th Plan period 
when VAMBAY will be launched in full swing, the annual allocation will be 
Rs. 1000 crorcs which will be matched 
226 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
with a long-term loan by HUDCO of Rs.1000 crore on a 1:1 basis. interest of 
this loan will be the same as the rate of interest charged by HUDCO for 
EWS housing. State Government option to mobilize  its matching portion of 
50% from other sources, such as their own budget provision, resources of 
local bodies, loans from other agencies, contributions from beneficiaries or 
NGOs etc. In all cases, however, the Government of India subsidy will only 
be released after the States matching share of 50% has been released. Both the 
subsidy and the loan (when it is requi red) will be released by HUDCO. The 
funds will be released by HUDCO eith er to the State Urban Development 
Agency (SUDA), District Urban Development Agency (DUDA) or any other 
agency designated by the State Government. 
The implementation of VAMBAY will be dovetailed and synergised with 
other existing programmes such as NSDP and SJSRY. The availability of 
drinking water, sanitation and drainage facilities should be ensured under 
these programme. On an average, 25% of  the funds unde-the scheme will be 
spent for providing water and sanitation facilities including approximately 
20% of the amount for community sanitation project—Nirmal Bharat 
Abhiyan. 
Selection of beneficiaries will be made by the SUDA/DUDA in consultation 
with the local authorities. Help of reputed NGOs may be enlisted. They will 
also formulate projects, prepare estimates and submit the same for sanction 
to the State Government which will in turn recommend them to the 
Government of India for release of funds allocated for each State. 
In selecting the beneficiaries the following reservation/percentage will be 
followed: 
1. SC/ST 
2. Backward classes 
3. Other Weaker sections 
4. Physically & mentally 
disabled & handicapped 
persons and others 
 
—  not less than 50% 
—  30% 
—  15% (OBC, BC, Etc.) 
—  5% 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
After identification of the beneficiaries, the latter must be provided title as a 
pre-condition for the loan or subsidy. This may be done by the State 
Government/Local Body either by rcgularization in-situ or by relocation. The 
title to the land should be in the name of the husband and wife jointly or 
preferably in the name of the wife. Till the repayment of the loan, if any, the 
house built with VAMBAY funds along with the land shall be mortagaged to 
the State Government/implementing agency. It may please be noted that no 
provision is made for land acquisition in VAMBAY. No hard and fast 
type/design is prescribed for VAMBAY dwelling units. However, The plinth 
area of a new house should normally be not less than15   sq. mts. 
The upper financial limit for construction of VAMBAY units normally will 
be Rs. 40,000/- with provision for sanitary toilet also. However, for metro cities 
with more than 1-million population, it will be Rs. 50,000/- and mega cities 
(Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad and Bangalore) it will be Rs. 
60,000/- per unit. In hilly and difficult areas this celling may be enhanced by 
12.5%. A portion, say, 20% of the funds may be used also for upgrading 
existing dwelling units in slums. The upper limit for upgradation of an existing 
unit shall not be more than 50% of the ceiling specified for construction of a 
new house. The norms for Town & Country Planning of the State 
Government and the rules and bye-laws of the Local Bodies should, of 
course, be kept in view. 
Monitoring of VAMBAY will be done by the State Government and status 
report submitted to GOI regularly. 
Entitlement of State/UT under VAMBAY will be initially determined on 
the basis of slum population in the State or UT. The State Governments arc 
required to allocate the share for cities and towns within the State/UT also on 
the same norm i.e. in proportion to the slum population as a percentage of the 
total slum population of the State. 
The detailed proposals with cost estimates will be processed and submitted 
by HUDCO to a Committee headed by  the Secretary, Deptt. of Urban 
Employment & Poverty Alleviation, Ministry of Urban Development & 
Poverty Alleviation. If, however, sufficient 
228 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
proposals under VAMBAY are not forthcoming from some of the States, the 
balance funds can be reallocated to other States which have submitted their 
proposals.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) An extract of the guidelins issued by the Ministry of 
Urban Development on 14.1.1992, to prevent arbitrary use of powers to evict 
tenants from public premises is enclosed as Statement (See below). 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) and (e) Certain representations ha ve been received from some Tenants 
Associations in the past, alleging misuse of the provisions of Public Premises 
(Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 in general by some Public.

229 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March,  2002] 
Statement 
Extracts   of  Guidelines   Dated   14.1.1992   Formulated   to   Prevent 
Arbitrary use of Power to Evict Tenants from Public Premises 
(i) The provisions of the P.P. Act should be used primarily to evict totally 
illegal occupants of the premises of public authorities or unauthorised 
subletees, or employees who have ceased to be in their service and thus 
ineligible for occupatio n of the premises. The proceedings should be 
initiated in accordance with the provi sions of the Act only in cases 
where the occupation becomes unauthorised on genuine grounds of 
law. 
(ii) The provisions of the Act should not be resorted to either with a 
commercial motive or to secure vaca nt possession of the premises in 
order to accommodate their own employees, where the premises were 
in occupation of the original tenants to whom the premises were let 
either by the public authorities or the persons from whom the premises 
were acquired. 
(iii) A person in lawful occupation of  any premises should not be treated 
or declared to be an unauthorised occupant merely on service of 
notice of termination of tenancy, nor should any contractual 
agreement be wound up by taking advantage of the provisions of the 
Act. At the same time, it will be open to the public authority to secure 
periodic revision of rent in terms of the provisions of the Rent 
Control Act in each Stale or to move under genuine grounds under 
the Rent Control Act for resuming possession. In other words, the 
public authorities would have rights similar to private landlords under 
the Rent Control Act in dealing with genunine legal tenants. 
(iv) It is necessary to give no room for allegations that evictions were 
selectively resorted to for the purpose of securing an unwarranted 
increase in rent, or that a change in tenancy was permitted in order to 
avoid such imputations or abuses of discretionary powers. The 
release of premises or change of tenancy should be decided at the 
level of Board of Directors of the Public Undertakings. 
230 

[18 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) All the Public Undertakings should immediately review all pending 
cases before the Estate Officer or Courts with reference to these 
guidelines, and withdraw eviction proceedings against genuine 
tenants on grounds otherwise than as provided under these guidelines. 
The provisions under the P.P. Act should be used henceforth only in 
accordance with these guidelines.

DEVELOPMENT AND. POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (d) Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of 
Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT), selected 
small and medium towns within the population of 5 lakhs as per 1991 census 
are given Central assistance based on the detailed project reports submitted 
by State Governments in accordance with the prevailing guidelines of the 
scheme. Muzaffarpur, which is a Category 'D' town (population being

programmes; and 
(d) the performance made during last three years under these schemes? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation has been implementing a Centrally sponsored urban poverty 
alleviation programme called "Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY)" 
with effect from 1.12.1997 on all India basis to provide gainful employment to 
the urban unemployed or underemployed poor (i) through encouraging the setting 
up of self-employment ventures by those who have read upto 9th standard and (ii) 
through provision of wage employment by utilising their labour for construction of 
socially and economically useful public assets. The scheme is funded in the 
ratio of 75:25 between the Centre and the States. 
(b) Under SJSRY, main thrust is to give training and to help urban 
unemployed or underemployed poor who have read upto 9th 
standard through encouraging the setting up of self-employment 
ventures and also through provision of wage employment by utilising 
their labour for construction of socially and economically useful 
public assets whereas, Sampooma Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) 
is being implemented with effect from 25.9.2001 by the Ministry of 
Rural Development for the benefit of rural poor, both Below Poverty 
Line'lBPL) and Above Poverty Line (APL) who are in need of wage 
employment and are willing to take up manual/unskilled work by 
providing additional wage employment and also food security. 
(c) SJSRY is being implemented through the State/UT 
Governments. 
(d) Under SJSRY, based on the reports received from the State 
Govemments/UTs till 31.1.2002, 3.89 lakh urban poor have been 
assisted through setting up of micro enterprises, 3.48 lakhs have 
received training and 367.39 lakhs mandays of work have been 
generated with the utilisation of funds amounting to Rs. 831 crores 
(approximately).

STATEMENT BY MINISTERS 
Recently concluded Common Wealth Summit in Australia 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise to in form the hon. Members about the recent 
CHOGM, 2002, at Coolum in Australia. I had the honour to represent the hon. 
Prime Minister at this Conference - the first Commonwealth Summit in the 21 s1 
Century. 
The Commonwealth Heads of Government met in Coolum from March 
2nd to 5th, 2002, chaired by the Prim e Minister of Australia. The opening 
ceremony was addressed by Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, Head of the 
Commonwealth. The Heads of Government adopted the Commonwealth 
Coolum Declaration and a separate stat ement attached to the Declaration on 
Zimbabwe as well as the Coolum Communique. 
The Communique takes into account our major concerns, notably on 
terrorism and development. The Heads of Government reiterated their total 
condemnation of all acts of terrorism "in whatever for-m or wherever they occur 
or by whomsoever perpetrated", adding that there is "no justification for 
terrorism". Similarly, on multilateral tr ade issues, where a consensus is usually 
elusive, India was able to ensure that the language on WTO-related issues 
faithfully reflects the outcome at Doha and is supportive of the development 
agenda. 
280 

[18 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
The Coolum CHOGM also considered the issue of Zimbabwe. The 
discussions in the restricted Retreat indi cated different views on this matter, a 
consensus being in favour of postponin g action until after the receipt of the 
report of the Commonwealth Observer Group on the Presidential elections. At 
the same time, the Commonwealth leaders were not in favour of any dilution 
of its principles in support of democracy. 
The CHOGM statement on Zimbabwe, agreed to determine 
appropriate action on Zimbabwe, in the event that the Commonwealth 
Observer Group reported adversely. This consensus, in fact, emerged after 
India suggested closure of the debate urgi ng that this issue should not further 
divide the Commonwealth on ethnic and racial lines. 
One of the significant achievem ents at the Conference was the 
unanimous recommendation that India sh ould be invited to join CMAG (the 
Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group). As mentioned in the Coolum 
communique, India would become a member of the CMAG with immediate 
effect until the next CHOGM, along wi th Australia, Bahamas, Bangladesh, 
Botswana, Malta, Nigeria and Samoa. At the last meeting of the CMAG, 
endorsed by this CHOGM, Heads of Government agreed that Pakistan's 
suspension from the Councils of Commonwealth should remain unchanged 
pending the restoration of a democra tic Government. On Fiji, Heads of 
Government took note of the progress made in the restoration of democracy 
and endorsed CMAG's decision to lift Fiji' s suspension from the Councils of 
the Commonwealth. However, in recognition of the ongoing legal proceedings 
over the constitutionality of the Govern ment of Fiji it was agreed that CMAG 
should keep Fiji on its agenda. 
The President of Nigeria having offered to host the next CHOGM, the 
next Summit will be held in Nigeria in 2003. 
The outcome of the Conference ha s been entirely satisfactory from 
our perspective. The Coolum Declaration will help to advance the 
development agenda, while its robust st and on terrorism entirely takes into 
account our concerns. Our membership of CMAG over the next four years 
reinforces the strong position of India within the Commonwealth. 
Sir, with your permission, I would like to inform the hon. Members 
that the clarifications co uld, perhaps, be sought on Friday, and I will happily 
answer them. Thank you.

Sir, finally, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Finance

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Revision in the prices of domestic LPG 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): Sir, as the hon. Members are aw are, the Finance Minister had, in his 
Budget Speech, on 28 lh February, 2002, announced in this August House a 
reduction in the retail prices of diesel by around 50 paise per litre and of petrol 
by around Re. 1 per litre. Increases in the retail price of domestic LPG by 
about Rs.40 per cylinder and of Kerosene oil under Public Distribution System 
by around Rs.1.50 per litre were also announced. These changes in prices 
were given effect to by the oil companies with effect from 181 March, 2002. 
After the revision in the consumer prices that I have just now 
mentioned,   hon.   Prime   Minister   received   representations   from   various 
321 

RAJYA SABHA [18 MARCH, 2002]  
sections of society, including political parties and consumers groups. They had 
requested the Government for reducing the burden on consumers due to the 
recent increase in price of domestic LPG. The Government, after considering 
all aspects of the matter, have now decided to reduce theth retail selling price 
of domestic LPG by about Rs.20 per cy linder. This would be.nefi over 6.3 
crore urban and rural households using LP G for cooking. The reduction in the 
price has come into force from the midnight of I6th March, 2002. 
I may mention here that the oil prices, over last few weeks, have 
been showing an upward trend. The pr ice of Brent Crude Oil, which was 
around US $ 20 per barrel in the last w eek of February 2002, is presently over 
US $ 23 per barrel. The prices of petr oleum products in the international 
market have also moved upwards over past three weeks. In spite of the 
increase in the oil prices in the inte rnational market, the Government have, 
with a view to reduce the burden on consumers using LPG for cooking, 
decided to reduce the prices that I have just now mentioned. The subsidy 
burden due to this price reduction would increase by around Rs. 700 crores 
during the year 2002-03. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR): Mr. Dipankar 
Mukherjee. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, well, it is good that a reduction has been announced. I have three or four 
clarifications to seek from the hon. Minister. I feel he need ndt be apologetic to 
the Finance Minister for the so-called subsidy of around Rs. 700 crores more 
for this. 
My first point is: the Administered Price Mechanism has been 
removed as per the policy of the Un ited Front Government. Did they not 
suggest, specifically, a revision in the tax structure? In a sense, the road plan,' 
which has been placed before Parliament by the then Petroleum Minister, 
envisaged a 0.5 per cent import duty which now, actually, is 10 per cent. The 
excise duty on LPG and Kerosene was to be 10 per cent, as per that road 
map, which is now, if I am not mistak en, is 16 per cent. Sir, the hon. Finance 
Minister is frowning at me. With this 5 per cent and 6 per cent increase in 
excise duty, how much money is been going to the Finance Ministry?   If the 
road map for the APM is implemented, as per the decision 
322 

[18 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
of the United Front Government, then,  why was not the tax revision on both 
import duty and excise duty not'been followed in toto? This is my first point. 
How do you say that once your import is  high, your excise duty is high, the 
subsidy will also go up? In 1993, when  the price of Kerosene was Rs. 1.5 per 
litre and the LPG was Rs. no per cylinder, the subsidy amount was Rs. 5,043 
crores. Today, when the cost of an LPG cylinder is Rs. 267 or 287 -- if you 
take into account the increased amount of Rs. 40 per cylinder -- and kerosene 
is Rs. 9.50, the subsidy component is st ill Rs. 6,000 crores. The major part is, 
the tax and the duty structure has not been revised. Had that revision been 
done, as per the decision of the U.F. Government, would this increase in prices 
have become necessary? 
My second point is, there is a recommendation of the Standing 
Committee on this. The international price of crude oil is increasing. So far as 
the indigenous oil is concerned, a cess of Rs. 900 per tonne was being 
charged, which, this time, has been increased to Rs. 1,800 per tonne. This 
cess, as per the Act, envisaged, will be ut ilised for the development of oil and 
petroleum sectors, including fertilizer. So , now, the record says that up to 
March, 2000 -- if I am not mistaken -- Rs. 32,000 crores was collected towards 
cess. Out of that Rs. 902 crores were given to the Industrial Development 
Board. Right now, you say it will be the market that will determine the price. If it 
is the market-determined price, if it is a free market, then, this cess, which has 
been increased by Rs. 9000/- per tonne, would generate Rs. 2,700 crores 
excess this year. This Rs. 2,700 crores, fo r what it would Joe utilized? Who is 
subsidising whom? This money is going to the Consolidated Fund of India. It 
means Rs. 2,700 crores is going extra. But this is a charge on which the 
subsidy is also increasing. How do yo u then justify a market economy? The 
Government says, "We are not involved in investment. Private investment will 
come." When the private investments are coming, then, why only indigenous 
oil producers are being levied the cess? The cess is being charged only from 
the public sector units, that is, Oil India Ltd. and  ONGC. The private sector 
companies are not being charged any cess. Then, with the increase in cess, 
naturally, the subsidy amount is also in creasing. So, why this cess is there? 
You remove "i that. Revive the tax structure. I am sure you will not have to do 
this subsidy calculation at the end. You bring up the import duty by 10 per cent, 
and bring down the excise duty to 8 per cent. See how much is your actual 
subsidy. The subsidy calculation must be open and transparent to the people 
of this country.   Just giving the figures is not sufficient. It should 
323 

RAJYA SABHA [18 MARCH, 2002]  
be clear -- right from the crude oil prices , both indigenous as well as imported 
oil -- how the retail prices are being fixed, how the subsidy is being' contained. 
That should be on record in the Parlia ment. The Parliament can decide on it. 
And the cess collected for the oil industry development, should not be used for 
making up the fiscal deficit.

DR.   ARUN   KUMAR   SARMA:      Every  year,   there   is   a iget  
everywhere giving the total receipts and expenditure as also the ref that have 
taken place in recent years. Generally speaking, I welcome this Budget. But 
the common criticism is t hat the Budget is more pro-rich than helping the 
poorer section of the society. In the earlier Budgets, this was taken care of. 
For three consecutive years, after the pay revision, the problem of the salaried 
class, who come under the upper slab of the tax structure, was not taken care 
of. We hope, at least, this time the hon.  Finance Minister will consider that 
point. The taxation limit of the salaried class, who come under the upper slab 
of the tax structure, has not been re-evaluated for three consecutive years. In 
the last year's Budget, there was a wide gap between the estimated receipts 
and expenditure and the actual receipts and expenditure. We are just showing 
to the nation that we are going to ear n so much through tax collection and 
other sources of revenue and we are going to implement a lot of programmes. 
If we really assess the previous year's Budget, the receipts were far less than 
what was expected. I have just evalua ted certain items. When I evaluated 
many of the parameters, I found that the actual re ceipts under a particular 
item were only 10 per cent or 15 per ce nt as against the estimated 25 per 
cent. So, this is only some kind of a calculation to give an impression to the 
people that something will happen in future or in the coming years. It docs not 
really happen. 
Sir, I happened to meet a former Secretary in the Ministry of Finance. 
He was heading the Department of Expenditure. It was very hurting to note 
that in many cases the money, even thou gh it is budgeted, is not released in 
the real sense. If you go to many of the Departments, you will find that many 
files, many proposals, from different Departments are pending with the Finance 
Ministry. Even at the end of the financ ial year, many budgetary proposals of 
various Departments are yet to be cleared by the Finance Ministry. I don't 
blame anybody. It is the system that the bureaucracy has created just to give 
an impression to the people that something will be done. Generally speaking, I 
welcome the hon. Finance Minister's Budget because I hail from the North-
Eastern Region. The Finance Minister ha s made two specific proposals in his 
Budget and indicated them in his Bu dget Speech. The entire House knows 
that the then hon. Prime Mi nister in 1996 declared that  10 per cent of the total 
budgetary allocation would be made to t he North-Eastern Region. This was a 
national programme. The North Eastern   MPs' Forum took a decision to

evaluate whether 10 per cent  of the budgetary provisions was really being 
invested in the North Eastern Region or not. Last year, we found that many 
Departments did not utilise even one per cent of the total budgetary provisions 
in the North Eastern Region, though they declared that they are allocating 10 
per cent of the budgetary provisions. We demanded that a survey should be 
conducted to find out as to how many Departments have allocated 10 per cent 
of their budgetary provisions. Sir, al though the hon. Finance Minister has 
given an estimate that Rs. 5,000 crores have been allocated by the various 
Central Ministries for spending in the North East, this amount is not even 5 per 
cent of the total budget ary provisions. The present NDA Government has 
formulated another scheme. Many of t he Departments have made budgetary 
allocation for the North Eastern Region,  but they have not been able to utilise 
the money for various reasons. There wa s a provision that the entire unspent 
money would be shifted to the Non-Lapsable Pool so that if the allocated 
money is not utilised, then that money coul d be utilised next year. But it is a 
hard fact to know that till today, the amount which has gone to the Non-
Lapsable Pool is only Rs. 500 crores. Some Departments have neither 
allocated 10 per cent of their budget fo r the North East, nor have they utilised 
the money and nor have they transferr ed the unspent amount to the Non-
Lapsable Pool. They are saying that a huge amount of money is being 
allocated to the North Eastern Region fr om the Central fund. But, nothing is 
coming. I would request the Government to review the promise which has 
been made to the North Eastern Region; otherwise, a wrong message would 
go to the people of the North Easter n Region. Everybody is aware of the 
situation in the North East. It is very frag ile. Sir, 98 per cent of the boundary of 
the North Eastern Region is surrounde d by the neighbouring countries. There 
are so many external forces which are working there. Insurgency has gone to 
the grassroots level. There is a gr eat need for a healing touch. The 
Government should start some employment generation programmes so that 
the youths could be brought to the mainstream. The present approach of the 
Government of India is not going to so lve the problems of the North Eastern 
Region. I hope the hon. Finance Minister would take a realistic view of the 
situation and would take special care of  this particular issue. I would also 
request the Finance Minister to hold a discussion with the Members of 
Parliament from the North Eastern Region. 
Here I would like to welcome the declaration made by the Finance 
Minister that every refinery in the North Eastern Region would be given 50 per 
cent  excise duty exemption.     Earlier,  the  Prime  Minister made an
